claim: α-Xenorhabdolysins (Xax) are α-pore-forming toxins (α-PFT) that form 1–1.3 MDa large pore complexes to perforate the host cell membrane.
source: α-Xenorhabdolysins (Xax) are α-pore-forming toxins (α-PFT) that form 1–1.3 MDa large pore complexes to perforate the host cell membrane.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and is supported by the structural data presented in the manuscript showing the pore complex structure.

claim: The cryo-EM structure of the XaxAB pore complex from Xenorhabdus nematophila was determined.
source: Here, we report the cryo-EM structure of the XaxAB pore complex from Xenorhabdus nematophila and the crystal structures of the soluble monomers of XaxA and XaxB.
evidence: The manuscript describes the determination of the cryo-EM structure with detailed methods and results.

claim: The crystal structures of the soluble monomers of XaxA and XaxB were determined.
source: Here, we report the cryo-EM structure of the XaxAB pore complex from Xenorhabdus nematophila and the crystal structures of the soluble monomers of XaxA and XaxB.
evidence: Crystal structures were solved to 2.5 Å for XaxA and 3.4 Å for XaxB as described in the results.

claim: XaxA and XaxB are built similarly and appear as heterodimers in the 12–15 subunits containing pore.
source: The structures reveal that XaxA and XaxB are built similarly and appear as heterodimers in the 12–15 subunits containing pore, classifying XaxAB as bi-component α-PFT.
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM structure showing heterodimers in pores with variable subunit numbers.

claim: XaxAB is classified as a bi-component α-PFT.
source: The structures reveal that XaxA and XaxB are built similarly and appear as heterodimers in the 12–15 subunits containing pore, classifying XaxAB as bi-component α-PFT.
evidence: The structural data showing both components contributing to the pore supports this classification.

claim: Major conformational changes in XaxB, including the swinging out of an amphipathic helix, are responsible for membrane insertion.
source: Major conformational changes in XaxB, including the swinging out of an amphipathic helix are responsible for membrane insertion.
evidence: Comparison of monomer and pore structures reveals conformational changes in XaxB's head domain.

claim: XaxA acts as an activator and stabilizer for XaxB that forms the actual transmembrane pore.
source: XaxA acts as an activator and stabilizer for XaxB that forms the actual transmembrane pore.
evidence: The structural arrangement and interactions between XaxA and XaxB support this functional interpretation.

claim: PFTs are used by a variety of bacterial pathogens to attack host cells.
source: PFTs are used by a variety of bacterial pathogens to attack host cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of bacterial pathogenesis.

claim: Pore-forming toxins (PFTs) are soluble proteins produced by bacteria and higher eukaryotes, that spontaneously form pores in biomembranes and act as toxins.
source: Pore-forming toxins (PFTs) are soluble proteins produced by bacteria and higher eukaryotes, that spontaneously form pores in biomembranes and act as toxins (Dal Peraro and van der Goot, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: PFTs are classified as α-PFTs and β-PFTs dependent on their transmembrane region, which is formed either by α-helices or β-strands.
source: Dependent on their transmembrane region, which is formed either by α-helices or β-strands, PFTs are classified as α-PFTs and β-PFTs (Iacovache et al., 2008; Bischofberger et al., 2012).
evidence: This classification is supported by citations to the literature.

claim: A common trait of all PFTs is the conversion from a soluble monomer to a membrane-embedded oligomer.
source: A common trait of all PFTs is the conversion from a soluble monomer to a membrane-embedded oligomer (Bischofberger et al., 2012); however, a different mechanism has been recently found for ABC toxins (Gatsogiannis et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the literature.

claim: ABC toxins have a different mechanism than the typical conversion from soluble monomer to membrane-embedded oligomer.
source: A common trait of all PFTs is the conversion from a soluble monomer to a membrane-embedded oligomer (Bischofberger et al., 2012); however, a different mechanism has been recently found for ABC toxins (Gatsogiannis et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a specific study on ABC toxins.

claim: Specific targeting of the PFTs to the host membrane involves mostly recognition of specific proteins, glycans or lipids on the target membrane.
source: Specific targeting of the PFTs to the host membrane involves mostly recognition of specific proteins, glycans or lipids on the target membrane.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PFT mechanisms.

claim: Conformational changes resulting in the oligomerization and membrane perforation are triggered by receptor binding, catalytic cleavage, pH change or other factors.
source: Conformational changes resulting in the oligomerization and membrane perforation are triggered by receptor binding, catalytic cleavage, pH change or other factors (Iacovache et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the literature.

claim: The size of the oligomers ranges from tetrameric pores in Cry1Aa to 30–50-meric pores in cholesterol-dependent cytolysins (CDCs).
source: The size of the oligomers ranges from tetrameric pores in Cry1Aa (Gómez et al., 2014) and heptameric pores in the anthrax protective antigen (Jiang et al., 2015) to 30–50-meric pores in cholesterol-dependent cytolysins (CDCs) (Dal Peraro and van der Goot, 2016; Hotze and Tweten, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to specific examples in the literature.

claim: PFTs of the first group perforate membranes by forming stable pores resulting in an uncontrolled influx and efflux of ions and other biomolecules.
source: PFTs of the first group perforate membranes by forming stable pores resulting in an uncontrolled influx and efflux of ions and other biomolecules.
evidence: This describes a known mechanism of one class of PFTs.

claim: The toxins of the second group perforate the membrane, but use the transmembrane channel to specifically translocate toxic enzymes into the host.
source: The toxins of the second group also perforate the membrane, but use the transmembrane channel to specifically translocate toxic enzymes into the host.
evidence: This describes a known mechanism of another class of PFTs.

claim: Binary toxins, also called AB toxins, and ABC toxins belong to the group of PFTs that translocate toxic enzymes.
source: Binary toxins, also called AB toxins (Odumosu et al., 2010) and also recently characterized ABC toxins (Meusch et al., 2014) belong to the latter group.
evidence: This is supported by citations to the literature.

claim: The anthrax toxin is a prominent AB toxin where component B forms a translocation pore through which lethal factor or edema factor are translocated.
source: A prominent AB toxin is the anthrax toxin (Collier and Young, 2003), where component B, the protective antigen, forms a translocation pore through which lethal factor or edema factor, different A components, are translocated.
evidence: This is supported by citation to the literature on anthrax toxin.

claim: The members of α-PFTs show a high structural diversity.
source: The members of α-PFTs show a high structural diversity.
evidence: This is established knowledge about α-PFTs.

claim: α-PFTs include proteins mainly consisting of α-helical structures or β-strand motifs with a single helix responsible for membrane insertion.
source: They include proteins mainly consisting of α-helical structures (bax, colicins) or β-strand motifs with a single helix responsible for membrane insertion (actinoporins) (Dal Peraro and van der Goot, 2016; Parker and Feil, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the literature.

claim: The transmembrane regions of α-PFTs are all composed of hydrophobic or amphipathic regions buried within the core structure of the soluble monomer.
source: Their transmembrane regions are all composed of hydrophobic or amphipathic regions buried within the core structure of the soluble monomer.
evidence: This is established knowledge about α-PFT structure.

claim: A conformational change that exposes the hydrophobic or amphipathic region is required for successful membrane insertion of α-PFTs.
source: Therefore, a conformational change that exposes the hydrophobic or amphipathic region is required for successful membrane insertion.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the structure of α-PFTs.

claim: The structures of cytolysin A (ClyA) and fragaceatoxin C (FraC) of both the monomer and oligomer gave the first structural insight into the mechanism of action of α-PFTs.
source: The structures of cytolysin A (ClyA) (Wallace et al., 2000; Mueller et al., 2009) and fragaceatoxin C (FraC) (Wallace et al., 2000; Mueller et al., 2009) of both the monomer and oligomer gave the first structural insight into the mechanism of action of this class of PFTs.
evidence: This is supported by citations to the literature.

claim: The structures of many β-PFTs have been determined in their monomeric and pore conformation.
source: In contrast to α-PFTs, the structures of many β-PFTs, such as members of the cholesterol-dependent cytolysins (Hotze and Tweten, 2012), hemolysin and aerolysin family (Dal Peraro and van der Goot, 2016), have been determined in their monomeric and pore conformation.
evidence: This is supported by citations to the literature.

claim: The transmembrane β-strands in the soluble monomers of β-PFTs are typically amphipathic with small hydrophobic patches that upon oligomerization form a hydrophobic membrane-spanning β-barrel.
source: The transmembrane β-strands in the soluble monomers of β-PFTs are typically amphipathic with small hydrophobic patches that upon oligomerization form a hydrophobic membrane-spanning β-barrel.
evidence: This is established knowledge about β-PFT structure.

claim: α-Xenorhabdolysin is a PFT that has been first isolated from the bacterium Xenorhabdus nematophila.
source: α-Xenorhabdolysin is a PFT that has been first isolated from the bacterium Xenorhabdus nematophila (Ribeiro et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the literature.

claim: Xenorhabdolysins are found in entomopathogenic bacteria such as Photorhabdus luminescens, and human pathogenic bacteria such as Yersinia enterocolitica and Proteus mirabilis.
source: Xenorhabdolysins are also found in other entomopathogenic bacteria, such as Photorhabdus luminescens, and human pathogenic bacteria, such as Yersinia enterocolitica and Proteus mirabilis (Vigneux et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the literature.

claim: Xenorhabdolysins are composed of two subunits, namely XaxA (45 kDa) and XaxB (40 kDa).
source: They are composed of two subunits, namely XaxA (45 kDa) and XaxB (40 kDa) and are only active when the two components act together (Vigneux et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the literature.

claim: Xenorhabdolysins are only active when the two components act together.
source: They are composed of two subunits, namely XaxA (45 kDa) and XaxB (40 kDa) and are only active when the two components act together (Vigneux et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the literature.

claim: Xenorhabdolysins perforate the membranes of erythrocytes, insect granulocytes and phagocytes and induce apoptosis.
source: Xenorhabdolysins, which were suggested to be binary toxins (Vigneux et al., 2007; Zhang et al., 2014), perforate the membranes of erythrocytes, insect granulocytes and phagocytes and induce apoptosis (Vigneux et al., 2007; Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the literature.

claim: Xenorhabdolysins were suggested to be binary toxins.
source: Xenorhabdolysins, which were suggested to be binary toxins (Vigneux et al., 2007; Zhang et al., 2014), perforate the membranes of erythrocytes, insect granulocytes and phagocytes and induce apoptosis (Vigneux et al., 2007; Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the literature, though the manuscript later refutes this classification.

claim: Structural prediction using the PHYRE2 server does not yield any significant similarities for XaxB.
source: Structural prediction using the PHYRE2 server (Kelley and Sternberg, 2009) does not yield any significant similarities for XaxB.
evidence: This is based on computational prediction analysis.

claim: XaxA cytotoxins are predicted to be similar to Cry6Aa from Bacillus thuringiensis and binding component B of hemolysin BL (Hbl-B) from Bacillus cereus.
source: XaxA cytotoxins, however, are predicted to be similar to two pore-forming cytolysins, Cry6Aa from Bacillus thuringiensis (Huang et al., 2016) and binding component B of hemolysin BL (Hbl-B) from Bacillus cereus (Madegowda et al., 2008).
evidence: This is based on structural prediction and citations to the literature.

claim: ClyA is the best characterized cytolysin.
source: The best characterized cytolysin is probably ClyA from Escherichia coli and Salmonella enterica strains.
evidence: This is a statement based on the extent of literature on ClyA.

claim: The structure of ClyA has been determined in its soluble form and pore conformation.
source: The structure of ClyA has been determined in its soluble form (Wallace et al., 2000) and pore conformation (Mueller et al., 2009) and the mechanism of pore formation mechanism has been extensively studied (Roderer and Glockshuber, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the literature.

claim: ClyA only contains one component, in contrast to XaxAB.
source: However, in contrast to XaxAB, ClyA only contains one component.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ClyA structure.

claim: Despite the structural similarity between ClyA and XaxAB, the mechanism of action must be different.
source: Thus, despite the structural similarity, the mechanism of action must be different.
evidence: This is an inference based on the difference in component number.

claim: Structural data on xenorhabdolysins are missing, limiting our understanding of these important type of toxins.
source: So far structural data on xenorhabdolysins are missing limiting our understanding of these important type of toxins.
evidence: This statement is made prior to the presentation of the new structures in this manuscript.

claim: The crystal structure of XaxA was solved to 2.5 Å resolution.
source: We obtained well diffracting crystals of both XaxA and XaxB in their soluble monomeric form and solved their structures to 2.5 and 3.4 Å, respectively (Figure 1a–b, Table 1).
evidence: This is reported in the results section with supporting data in Table 1.

claim: The crystal structure of XaxB was solved to 3.4 Å resolution.
source: We obtained well diffracting crystals of both XaxA and XaxB in their soluble monomeric form and solved their structures to 2.5 and 3.4 Å, respectively (Figure 1a–b, Table 1).
evidence: This is reported in the results section with supporting data in Table 1.

claim: Both XaxA and XaxB have a long rod-shaped structure and are mainly composed of α-helices.
source: Both XaxA and XaxB have a long rod-shaped structure and are mainly composed of α-helices (Figure 1a–b).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structures.

claim: XaxA and XaxB have a similar domain organization.
source: XaxA and XaxB have a similar domain organization.
evidence: This is observed from the crystal structures.

claim: Both XaxA and XaxB contain a tail domain that is formed by a five-helix bundle (αA, αB, αC, αG and αH) and elongated neck and head domains.
source: They both contain a tail domain that is formed by a five-helix bundle (αA, αB, αC, αG and αH) and elongated neck and head domains.
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structures.

claim: The five-helix bundle motif has so far only been described for ClyA and ClyA-type toxins.
source: The five-helix bundle motif has so far only been described for ClyA and ClyA-type toxins (Roderer and Glockshuber, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the literature.

claim: The N-terminal helices (αA) of XaxA and XaxB are significantly shorter than in ClyA.
source: Like in the case of ClyA-type toxins the N-terminal helices (αA) of XaxA and XaxB are significantly shorter than in ClyA, where it plays a crucial role in pore formation (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is observed by comparing the structures.

claim: XaxA contains two large loops connecting the helices: a hook-shaped loop (lp1, aa 136–169) between helices αB and αC and an additional loop (lp2, aa 202–215) dividing helix αC.
source: Interestingly, XaxA contains two large loops connecting the helices, a big hook-shaped loop (lp1, aa 136–169) between helices αB and αC at the top of the tail domain and an additional loop (lp2, aa 202–215) dividing helix αC (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure of XaxA.

claim: The four XaxB molecules in the asymmetric unit differ considerably in their tail domain.
source: The four XaxB molecules in the asymmetric unit differ considerably in their tail domain (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure of XaxB.

claim: Helices αB and αC of XaxB that protrude slightly from the five-helix-bundle take different positions.
source: Especially, helices αB and αC that protrude slightly from the five-helix-bundle take different positions.
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure of XaxB.

claim: The variability in XaxB tail domain positions might be due to tight crystal packing or indicates flexibility of the tail domain.
source: Although this might be due to tight crystal packing, it also indicates a certain degree of flexibility of the tail domain of XaxB.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the crystallographic observations.

claim: A long coiled-coil structure connects all domains and forms the neck and head domain in both XaxA and XaxB.
source: A long coiled-coil structure, composed of a continuous helix (αG) and another one that is divided into three (XaxA: αC1, αC2 and αD) or two (XaxB: αC, αD) segments, form the backbone of XaxA and XaxB. It connects all domains and forms in both XaxA and XaxB the neck and head domain.
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structures.

claim: The neck domain is approximately 35 Å in length and does not exist in ClyA-type toxins.
source: The neck domain, that is approximately 35 Å in length, does not exist in ClyA-type toxins, which are in general more compact (Figure 1—figure supplement 4a).
evidence: This is observed by comparing structures.

claim: In XaxA, the tip of the coiled-coil, predicted as hydrophobic transmembrane region, is not resolved in the crystal structure.
source: In XaxA, the tip of the coiled-coil, predicted as hydrophobic transmembrane region is not resolved in our crystal structure, however, secondary structure predictions for this region suggest a continuation of the coiled-coil (Figure 1—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure and supported by secondary structure prediction.

claim: The head domain of XaxB contains a helix-loop-helix motif dividing helix αE and a 21-residue long amphipathic helix (αF).
source: In contrast to XaxA the head domain of XaxB contains in addition to the central coiled-coil a helix-loop-helix motif, dividing helix αE and a 21-residue long amphipathic helix (αF).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure of XaxB.

claim: The highly conserved hydrophobic face of helix αF is oriented toward helices αD and αG and thereby shielded from the solvent.
source: The highly conserved hydrophobic face of helix αF is oriented toward helices αD and αG and thereby shielded from the solvent (Figures 1b and 2).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure of XaxB.

claim: The conformation of the head domain of XaxB is stabilized by conserved hydrophobic as well as electrostatic interactions, including putative salt bridges.
source: The conformation of the head domain is stabilized by conserved hydrophobic as well as electrostatic interactions, including putative salt bridges (Figure 2).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure of XaxB.

claim: The overall fold of the soluble monomers is similar to that of ClyA from Escherichia coli or ClyA-type toxins.
source: In general, the overall fold of the soluble monomers is similar to that of ClyA from Escherichia coli (Wallace et al., 2000) or ClyA-type toxins, such as Cry6Aa from Bacillus thuringiensis (Huang et al., 2016), non-hemolytic enterotoxin A (NheA) (Ganash et al., 2013), and binding component B of hemolysin BL (Hbl-B) from Bacillus cereus (Madegowda et al., 2008) (Figure 1—figure supplement 4a).
evidence: This is observed by structural comparison and supported by citations.

claim: An important feature of ClyA and ClyA-type cytotoxins is the typical tongue motif that inserts into the membrane during pore formation.
source: An important feature of ClyA and ClyA-type cytotoxins is the typical tongue motif that inserts into the membrane during pore formation (Mueller et al., 2009) (Figure 1—figure supplement 4a,b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the literature.

claim: In ClyA, Hbl-B, NheA, and Cry6Aa the tongue is formed by a hydrophobic or amphipathic β-hairpin or a large hydrophobic loop.
source: In ClyA, Hbl-B, NheA, and Cry6Aa the tongue is formed by a hydrophobic or amphipathic β-hairpin or a large hydrophobic loop (Wallace et al., 2000; Huang et al., 2016; Madegowda et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the literature.

claim: In XaxB the tongue is formed by an amphipathic helix, while XaxA does not contain such motif.
source: Interestingly, in the case of XaxB the tongue is formed by an amphipathic helix, while XaxA does not contain such motif.
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structures.

claim: Comparing the structure of XaxA with that of its pore conformation suggests that XaxA is already in its extended conformation as soluble monomer.
source: Comparing the structure of XaxA with that of its pore conformation (see below) suggests that XaxA is already in its extended conformation as soluble monomer.
evidence: This is based on structural comparison between monomer and pore forms.

claim: The function of the N-terminal helix and β-tongue in ClyA has been evolutionary compensated in multicomponent toxins such as XaxAB, NheABC and Hbl-ABC that only contain a short N-terminal helix.
source: It is tempting to speculate that the function of the N-terminal helix and β-tongue in ClyA has been evolutionary compensated in multicomponent toxins, such as XaxAB, NheABC and Hbl-ABC that only contain a short N-terminal helix.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on structural comparisons.

claim: In XaxAB, the hydrophobic helices of XaxA that enter the membrane in the pore are functionally equivalent to the hydrophobic β-tongue of ClyA.
source: In the case of XaxAB, the hydrophobic helices of XaxA that enter the membrane in the pore, are functionally equivalent to the hydrophobic β-tongue of ClyA, The β-tongue likely inserts first into the membrane, where it rearranges into two α-helices (Mueller et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on structural and functional comparisons.

claim: αF and the helix-turn-helix motif αE of XaxB, that span the complete membrane in the XaxAB pore, would substitute the N-terminal membrane-spanning helix of ClyA.
source: Similar to XaxA, these helices only span half the membrane. αF and the helix-turn-helix motif αE of XaxB, that span the complete membrane in the XaxAB pore, would substitute the N-terminal membrane-spanning helix of ClyA.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on structural comparisons.

claim: The choice of detergent greatly influenced the size and homogeneity of the observed crown-shaped pore complexes.
source: We could indeed observe pore formation in most cases; however, the choice of detergent greatly influenced the size and homogeneity of the observed crown-shaped pore complexes.
evidence: This is observed experimentally during pore reconstitution.

claim: The most homogenous distribution of XaxAB pore complexes was observed after incubating the monomers with 0.1% Cymal-6.
source: We observed the most homogenous distribution of XaxAB pore complexes, that appear as crown-shaped structures, after incubating the monomers with 0.1% Cymal-6 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1c, Figure 3—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: This is observed experimentally during pore reconstitution.

claim: The average diameter of the XaxAB pores formed in Cymal-6 was ~250 Å.
source: The average diameter of the pores was ~250 Å.
evidence: This is measured from electron microscopy images.

claim: When soluble monomers of XaxA and XaxB were incubated in the absence of detergents at room temperature, the formation of higher oligomers but not of complete pores was observed.
source: Interestingly, when we incubated soluble monomers of XaxA and XaxB in the absence of detergents at room temperature, we observed the formation of higher oligomers but not of complete pores (Figure 1—figure supplement 3a,b).
evidence: This is observed experimentally.

claim: Heterodimerization and oligomerization of XaxAB can happen independently of the hydrophobic environment provided by detergents or a lipid bilayer.
source: This indicates that heterodimerization and oligomerization of XaxAB can happen independently of the hydrophobic environment provided by detergents or a lipid bilayer and may happen prior to pore formation also in vivo.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of oligomer formation without detergents.

claim: Most of the XaxAB pore complexes contain either 12, 13, 14 or 15 subunits.
source: Analyzing the single particles by two-dimensional clustering and sorting in SPHIRE (Yang et al., 2012; Moriya et al., 2017) revealed populations of XaxAB pores with different numbers of subunits (Figure 3—figure supplement 3). Most of the complexes contain either 12, 13, 14 or 15 subunits.
evidence: This is observed from cryo-EM image analysis.

claim: The average resolutions of the reconstructions were 5, 4, 4.2 and 4.3 Å for do-, tri-, tetra-, and pentadecameric pores, respectively.
source: The average resolutions of the reconstructions were 5, 4, 4.2 and 4.3 Å for do-, tri-, tetra-, and pentadecameric pores, respectively (Figure 3—figure supplements 4–5).
evidence: This is determined from cryo-EM reconstruction.

claim: The highest resolved cryo-EM density of the tridecameric pore complex was used to build an atomic model of XaxAB.
source: We used the highest resolved cryo-EM density of the tridecameric pore complex to build an atomic model of XaxAB (Video 1, Figure 3, Table 2).
evidence: This is described in the methods and results.

claim: The first residues of the N-terminal helix αA in XaxA (aa 1–40) and XaxB (aa 1–12) are not resolved in the cryo-EM structure.
source: The high quality of the map allowed both models to be almost completely built, except for the first residues of the N-terminal helix αA in XaxA (aa 1–40) and XaxB (aa 1–12).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The N-terminal regions not resolved in the cryo-EM structure are also not resolved in the crystal structures, indicating high flexibility of the N-termini.
source: These regions are also not resolved in the crystal structures indicating a high flexibility of the N-termini.
evidence: This is inferred from both crystal and cryo-EM structures.

claim: The pore complexes have a total height of 160 Å and depending on the number of subunits a diameter of 210 to 255 Å.
source: The pore complexes have a total height of 160 Å and depending on the number of subunits a diameter of 210 to 255 Å.
evidence: This is measured from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: Each subunit consists of a XaxAB heterodimer with XaxA bound to the back of XaxB.
source: Each subunit consists of a XaxAB heterodimer with XaxA bound to the back of XaxB.
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: XaxA is localized on the periphery of the pore, whereas XaxB resides more at the center of the complex lining the inner pore lumen.
source: This results in a localization of XaxA on the periphery of the pore, whereas XaxB resides more at the center of the complex lining the inner pore lumen (Figure 3, Video 1).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The transmembrane helices of XaxA do not completely span the membrane.
source: Interestingly, the transmembrane helices of XaxA that fortify the inner ring of helices of XaxB, do not completely span the membrane (Figure 3—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The arrangement of the components clearly shows that XaxAB is not a binary toxin as suggested, but rather a bi-component toxin.
source: The arrangement of the components clearly shows that XaxAB is not a binary toxin as suggested (Vigneux et al., 2007; Zhang et al., 2014), but rather a bi-component toxin, such as BinAB from Lysinibacillus sphaericus (Colletier et al., 2016) and leukocidin A and B (LukGH and SF) from Staphylococcus aureus (Badarau et al., 2015) where both proteins contribute to building the pore.
evidence: This is inferred from the cryo-EM structure showing both components in the pore.

claim: The inner diameter of the pore narrows down from 140 to 170 Å at the membrane-distal part to 40–55 Å at the transmembrane region, depending on the number of subunits.
source: Depending on the number of subunits, the inner diameter of the pore narrows down from 140 to 170 Å at the membrane-distal part to 40–55 Å at the transmembrane region.
evidence: This is measured from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The inner surface of the pore is hydrophilic and mostly negatively charged suggesting a preference for positively charged ions and molecules.
source: The inner surface of the pore is hydrophilic and mostly negatively charged suggesting a preference for positively charged ions and molecules (Figure 3—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This is observed from electrostatic surface analysis of the structure.

claim: At the outside, the pore complex has a conserved highly hydrophobic band of 40 Å corresponding to the transmembrane region.
source: At the outside, the pore complex has a conserved highly hydrophobic band of 40 Å corresponding to the transmembrane region (Figure 3—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This is observed from hydrophobicity surface analysis of the structure.

claim: The hydrophobic band merges into a positively charged stretch formed by conserved arginine and lysine residues of XaxA (R290, K291, K293, K295, K301).
source: The hydrophobic band merges into a positively charged stretch that is formed by the conserved arginine and lysine residues of XaxA (R290, K291, K293, K295, K301) (Figure 3—figure supplements 7–8).
evidence: This is observed from the structure and sequence analysis.

claim: The conserved positively charged residues of XaxA likely interact with negatively charged lipid head groups of target membranes and thereby stabilize the pore complex in the lipid bilayer.
source: These residues likely interact with negatively charged lipid head groups of target membranes and thereby stabilize the pore complex in the lipid bilayer.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural location and charge of these residues.

claim: The crown-like structure of XaxA is shared by actinoporin FraC but not by ClyA.
source: When comparing the shape of XaxAB with that of the pores of FraC and ClyA, we found that the crown-like structure of XaxA is shared by actinoporin FraC (Tanaka et al., 2015) but not by ClyA (Mueller et al., 2009), where the extramembrane regions form a cylinder (Figure 3—figure supplement 9a).
evidence: This is observed by structural comparison.

claim: FraC and ClyA pores have a smaller diameter than the XaxAB pore, in agreement with the smaller number and size of subunits.
source: In agreement with the smaller number and size of subunits in FraC and ClyA, these pores have a smaller diameter than the XaxAB pore, and, in addition, FraC contains large β-sheets in the extramembrane region (Figure 3—figure supplement 9b).
evidence: This is observed by structural comparison.

claim: The lumen of all pores (XaxAB, FraC, ClyA) is negatively charged, suggesting the same preference for positively charged molecules.
source: Interestingly, the lumen of all pores is negatively charged (Figure 3—figure supplement 9c), suggesting the same preference for positively charged molecules.
evidence: This is observed from electrostatic surface analysis.

claim: The tail domains of XaxA and XaxB do almost not differ between the oligomeric pore conformation and soluble monomers.
source: The tail domains of XaxA and XaxB do almost not differ between the oligomeric pore conformation and soluble monomers.
evidence: This is observed by comparing the crystal and cryo-EM structures.

claim: The neck and head domains of XaxA are arranged similarly to the crystal structure, however, the coiled-coil is twisted by 15 Å and interacts with helices αB and αC of the adjacent XaxB.
source: The neck and head domains of XaxA are also arranged similarly to the crystal structure, however, the coiled-coil is twisted by 15 Å and interacts with helices αB and αC of the adjacent XaxB (Figure 4a,c, Figure 5).
evidence: This is observed by comparing the crystal and cryo-EM structures.

claim: The neck and head domains of XaxB differ considerably in comparison to the soluble monomer.
source: The neck and head domains of XaxB, however, differ considerably in comparison to the soluble monomer.
evidence: This is observed by comparing the crystal and cryo-EM structures.

claim: The amphipathic helix αF and the helix-loop-helix motif of XaxB fold out, thereby extending helices αD and αG forming the transmembrane region.
source: The amphipathic helix αF and the helix-loop-helix motif fold out, thereby extending helices αD and αG forming the transmembrane region (Figure 4b,d, Figure 5).
evidence: This is observed by comparing the crystal and cryo-EM structures.

claim: The tail and head domains of XaxA and XaxB mediate interactions between the proteins in the heterodimer.
source: The tail and head domains of XaxA and XaxB mediate interactions between the proteins in the heterodimer.
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: Four major interfaces were identified between XaxA and XaxB: two in the tail and two in the head domain region.
source: We identified four major interfaces, two in the tail and two in the head domain region.
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The interfaces between the tail domains are stabilized by several putative hydrogen bonds and electrostatic interactions between helices αG and the C-terminal helix αH of XaxA and helices αB, αC and the C-terminal helix αH of XaxB.
source: The interfaces between the tail domains are stabilized by several putative hydrogen bonds and electrostatic interactions between helices αG and the C-terminal helix αH of XaxA and helices αB, αC and the C-terminal helix αH of XaxB (Figure 5a–c).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: Dimerization of XaxA and XaxB probably helps stabilizing the tail domain of XaxB.
source: Dimerization of XaxA and XaxB probably helps stabilizing the tail domain of XaxB, which takes different positions in the crystal structure (Figure 5a, Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is inferred from the structural observations.

claim: The first interface between the head domains is formed by helices αD and αG of XaxA that interact with helices αD and αG of XaxB via a putative hydrogen network and salt bridges.
source: The first interface between the head domains is formed by helices αD and αG of XaxA that interact with helices αD and αG of XaxB via a putative hydrogen network and salt bridges (Figure 5d).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The second interface between head domains is mediated by hydrophobic interactions between helices αF and αE of XaxB with αD and αG of XaxA.
source: The second one is mediated by hydrophobic interactions between helices αF and αE of XaxB with αD and αG of XaxA (Figure 5f).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: A prominent feature is the high accumulation of aromatic residues at the interface between XaxA and XaxB head domains.
source: A prominent feature is the high accumulation of aromatic residues at this interface (Figure 5e).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: Some of the aromatic residues at the XaxA-XaxB interface are also involved in stabilizing the soluble XaxB monomer.
source: Interestingly, some of these residues are also involved in stabilizing the soluble XaxB monomer (Figure 2).
evidence: This is observed by comparing the crystal and cryo-EM structures.

claim: Since most of the interfaces between XaxA and XaxB in the heterodimer locate to the tail domain and do not differ between the soluble monomer and pore conformation, heterodimer formation precedes membrane insertion.
source: Since most of the interfaces between XaxA and XaxB in the heterodimer locate to the tail domain and do not differ between the soluble monomer and pore conformation, we suggest that heterodimer formation precedes membrane insertion.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural observations.

claim: The heterodimers are linked manifold in the oligomeric pore, with one XaxA interacting simultaneously with XaxA and XaxB of the adjacent heterodimer.
source: The heterodimers are linked manifold in the oligomeric pore. One XaxA interacts simultaneously with XaxA and XaxB of the adjacent heterodimer. The same is true for XaxB that interacts with both XaxA and XaxB of the adjacent heterodimer (Figure 6).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: Two major interfaces are mediated by the tail domains of XaxA and XaxB between adjacent heterodimers.
source: Two major interfaces are mediated by the tail domains of XaxA and XaxB (Figure 6a–c).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The residues K45, N50, E398, E402 and D333 that are conserved in XaxA form an extensive putative hydrogen network and salt bridges with helices αB (R48, Y52) and αC (D138, R147) of the adjacent XaxB.
source: The residues K45, N50, E398, E402 and D333 that are conserved in XaxA form an extensive putative hydrogen network and salt bridges with helices αB (R48, Y52) and αC (D138, R147) of the adjacent XaxB (Figure 6b).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: A second putative hydrogen network between helices αC2 and αG in XaxA and helices αD and αG in XaxB likely contributes to the stabilization of the oligomer.
source: A second putative hydrogen network between helices αC2 and αG in XaxA and helices αD and αG in XaxB likely contributes to the stabilization of the oligomer (Figure 6c).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The oligomer is further stabilized by a putative salt bridge between glutamate E206 in the loop between αC1 and αC2 of XaxA and lysine K405 in the C-terminal helix of neighboring XaxA.
source: The oligomer is further stabilized by a putative salt bridge between two XaxAs. Glutamate E206 in the loop between αC1 and αC2 of XaxA of one subunit interacts with lysine K405 in the C-terminal helix of neighboring XaxA (Figure 6d).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The fourth interface is formed by the head domains of two XaxBs via several putative hydrogen bonds (D197/S241 N192/K245).
source: The fourth interface is formed by the head domains of two XaxBs via several putative hydrogen bonds (D197/S241 N192/K245) (Figure 6e).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The heterodimeric subunits of the complex and the heterodimer itself are stabilized by strong interactions that guarantee a stable pore complex inside the membrane.
source: Taken together the heterodimeric subunits of the complex and the heterodimer itself are stabilized by strong interactions that guarantee a stable pore complex inside the membrane.
evidence: This is inferred from the multiple interfaces observed in the structure.

claim: XaxA alone has the tendency to form small aggregates by interacting with its head domain.
source: XaxA alone has the tendency to form small aggregates by interacting with its head domain (Figure 1—figure supplement 1d–e).
evidence: This is observed experimentally.

claim: The clustering of XaxA monomers is caused by mild hydrophobic interactions of the short hydrophobic region of the head domain.
source: Since the short hydrophobic region of the head domain resides inside the membrane in the pore complex, we believe that the clustering of XaxA monomers is caused by mild hydrophobic interactions of these regions.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural observations.

claim: The soluble monomeric form of XaxA has a certain affinity to the hydrophobic environment of biomembranes.
source: This again suggests that already the soluble monomeric form of XaxA has a certain affinity to the hydrophobic environment of biomembranes.
evidence: This is inferred from the aggregation behavior of XaxA.

claim: XaxA was not incorporated into POPC or BPL liposomes and no larger structures could be observed on the vesicles.
source: Interestingly, the protein was not incorporated into the liposomes and no larger structures could be observed on the vesicles (Figure 7c,d).
evidence: This is observed experimentally in reconstitution assays.

claim: XaxA cannot spontaneously insert blank membranes in vitro despite the hydrophobic tip of the head domain.
source: This indicates that albeit the hydrophobic tip of the head domain, XaxA cannot spontaneously insert blank membranes in vitro.
evidence: This is inferred from the reconstitution experiments.

claim: XaxB alone neither perforates membranes nor oligomerizes on liposomes when incubated with them.
source: The same is true for XaxB alone. When incubated with liposomes the protein neither perforates membranes nor oligomerizes on the liposomes (Figure 7a,b,e,f).
evidence: This is observed experimentally in reconstitution assays.

claim: When both XaxA and XaxB were added to liposomes, they spontaneously associated with the vesicles and formed the typical crown-shaped structures.
source: When both XaxA and XaxB were added to liposomes, they spontaneously associated with the vesicles and formed the typical crown-shaped structures (Figure 7g–i) as we have observed them in detergents (Figure 3—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is observed experimentally in reconstitution assays.

claim: Association of XaxAB with liposomes is independent of the sequence of mixing XaxA and XaxB.
source: Notably, this is independent of the sequence of mixing, that is XaxA can be added before XaxB or vice versa, suggesting that dimerization of XaxA and XaxB is necessary for spontaneous association of the proteins with the membrane and subsequent pore formation.
evidence: This is observed experimentally in reconstitution assays.

claim: Dimerization of XaxA and XaxB is necessary for spontaneous association of the proteins with the membrane and subsequent pore formation.
source: Notably, this is independent of the sequence of mixing, that is XaxA can be added before XaxB or vice versa, suggesting that dimerization of XaxA and XaxB is necessary for spontaneous association of the proteins with the membrane and subsequent pore formation.
evidence: This is inferred from the reconstitution experiments.

claim: Association of XaxAB with liposomes happens without specific lipids, such as cholesterol, or protein receptors at the membrane surface.
source: Importantly, association with liposomes happens without specific lipids, such as cholesterol, or protein receptors at the membrane surface.
evidence: This is observed experimentally using simple lipid compositions.

claim: The transition from the soluble monomer to the protomer does not involve major structural rearrangements of the whole molecule, only the conformation of the head domains changes considerably.
source: In general, the transition from the soluble monomer to the protomer does not involve major structural rearrangements of the whole molecule. Only the conformation of the head domains changes considerably.
evidence: This is observed by comparing the crystal and cryo-EM structures.

claim: The conformation of the coiled-coil backbone in XaxB remains unaltered during the transition from monomer to protomer.
source: Interestingly, the conformation of the coiled-coil backbone in XaxB remains unaltered (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is observed by comparing the crystal and cryo-EM structures.

claim: The conformational changes in XaxB are in direct contrast to ClyA but similar to FraC.
source: This is in direct contrast to ClyA (Wallace et al., 2000) but similar to FraC (Tanaka et al., 2015), the only other two α-PFTs, for which a structure of the soluble and pore complex has been determined at high resolution.
evidence: This is observed by structural comparison and supported by citations.

claim: In ClyA, not only the head domain but also the tail domain undergoes considerable conformational changes.
source: In ClyA, not only the head domain but also the tail domain undergoes considerable conformational changes (Mueller et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the literature.

claim: When the crystal structures of XaxA and XaxB are overlaid with the respective XaxAB structure, the neck and head domains of the proteins would not interact.
source: When the crystal structures of XaxA and XaxB are overlaid with the respective XaxAB structure, it becomes obvious that the neck and head domains of the proteins would not interact (Video 2).
evidence: This is observed by structural superposition.

claim: A dimer of XaxA and XaxB in their monomeric conformations would probably not be able to spontaneously insert into membranes.
source: In agreement with our reconstitution assays such a dimer would probably not be able to spontaneously insert into membranes.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural analysis and reconstitution experiments.

claim: In the XaxAB pore conformation, helices αD and αG of XaxA twist by 15 Å toward XaxB, creating a stronger interaction.
source: In the XaxAB pore conformation, however, helices αD and αG of XaxA, forming the coiled-coil backbone twist by 15 Å toward XaxB (Figure 4a, Figure 5, Video 2). As described above, through this conformational change a stronger interaction with XaxB is created.
evidence: This is observed by comparing the crystal and cryo-EM structures.

claim: Without the conformational change in XaxA, oligomerization of XaxAB would not be possible because of prominent steric hindrances.
source: Interestingly, without the conformational change in XaxA, oligomerization of XaxAB would not be possible because of prominent steric hindrances (Video 3).
evidence: This is inferred from structural modeling.

claim: The conformational change in XaxA is crucial for complex formation.
source: This movement is therefore crucial for complex formation.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural analysis.

claim: If only XaxA and not XaxB changed its conformation during dimerization and oligomerization, the transmembrane region of XaxA would sterically clash with the loop between αF and αG of XaxB from the adjacent subunit.
source: If we assumed that only XaxA and not XaxB changed its conformation during dimerization and oligomerization (Video 2, Video 3), the transmembrane region of XaxA would sterically clash with the loop between αF and αG of XaxB from the adjacent subunit (Videos 2 and 3).
evidence: This is inferred from structural modeling.

claim: The steric clash of XaxA with the loop between αF and αG of XaxB could trigger conformational changes in XaxB that activate its head domain for membrane insertion.
source: This could in principle trigger conformational changes in XaxB that activate its head domain for membrane insertion.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on structural modeling.

claim: Two hinge regions facilitate the swinging out movement of αF in XaxB.
source: We identified two hinge regions that facilitate the swinging out movement of αF in XaxB (Figure 8, Video 2, Video 3).
evidence: This is identified from structural analysis.

claim: One hinge region is located in the hydrophobic loop between the short helices of the helix-loop-helix motif and contains a highly conserved proline residue (P204).
source: One hinge region is located in the hydrophobic loop between the short helices of the helix-loop-helix motif. It contains a highly conserved proline residue (P204) that is also involved in stabilization of the soluble monomer (Figure 2).
evidence: This is identified from structural analysis.

claim: The second hinge is located in the loop connecting αF and αG, including the conserved residue G243.
source: The second hinge is located in the loop connecting αF and αG, including the conserved residue G243 (Figure 2, Figure 8).
evidence: This is identified from structural analysis.

claim: A cluster of aromatic residues at the bottom of the head domain of the XaxAprot-XaxBmon heterodimer model possibly triggers the conformational change of XaxB when exposed to a lipid membrane.
source: A cluster of aromatic residues at the bottom of the head domain of our XaxAprot-XaxBmon heterodimer model suggests that this region could be crucial in triggering the conformational changes in XaxB when exposed to a lipid membrane.
evidence: This is inferred from structural modeling.

claim: In the heterodimer of the XaxAB pore complex, most of the aromatic residues build a hydrophobic cluster between the transmembrane domain of XaxA and the reorganized helix αE of XaxB.
source: In the heterodimer of the XaxAB pore complex, most of these residues build a hydrophobic cluster between the transmembrane domain of XaxA and the reorganized helix αE of XaxB (Figure 8).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: Aromatic residues have been shown to be important for membrane insertion of many PFTs and responsible for conformational changes induced by their interaction with membranes or detergents.
source: Aromatic residues have been shown to be important for membrane insertion of many PFTs and responsible for conformational changes induced by their interaction with membranes or detergents (Mueller et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the literature.

claim: Interactions with the membrane likely destabilize the aromatic residue region, inducing stronger conformational changes in the rest of the domain.
source: Interactions with the membrane likely destabilize this region, inducing stronger conformational changes in the rest of the domain.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on structural analysis.

claim: XaxA and XaxB together form higher oligomers in the absence of detergent or membranes.
source: Our results show that XaxA and XaxB together form higher oligomers in the absence of detergent or membranes.
evidence: This is observed experimentally.

claim: XaxA likely activates XaxB during oligomerization by inducing conformational changes.
source: In addition, XaxA likely activates XaxB during oligomerization by inducing conformational changes.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural observations.

claim: XaxA and XaxB dimerize and oligomerize in solution.
source: We therefore propose that XaxA and XaxB dimerize (Figure 9a–c, Figure 9—figure supplements 1a–c and 2a–c) and oligomerize (Figure 9d, Figure 9—figure supplements 1d and 2d) in solution.
evidence: This is proposed based on the structural and experimental data.

claim: Dimerization of XaxA and XaxB happens probably spontaneously since the conformation of domains located at the heterodimer interface in the tail domains is not different compared to the monomers.
source: Dimerization happens probably spontaneously since the conformation of domains located at the heterodimer interface in the tail domains of XaxA and XaxB is not different compared to the monomers.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural observations.

claim: The conformational change in the neck and head domain of XaxA further stabilizes the interaction and is crucial for oligomerization.
source: The conformational change in the neck and head domain of XaxA (Figures 9b and 5d–f) further stabilizes the interaction and is crucial for oligomerization (Figure 9d).
evidence: This is inferred from the structural observations.

claim: During oligomerization XaxA sterically clashes with the loop connecting helices αF and αG in XaxB.
source: During oligomerization XaxA sterically clashes with the loop connecting helices αF and αG in XaxB.
evidence: This is inferred from structural modeling.

claim: XaxA induces conformational changes in XaxB that put XaxB in an activated state for membrane insertion.
source: We therefore propose that XaxA induces conformational changes in XaxB that do not immediately result in exposing its hydrophobic domain but rather put XaxB in an activated state for membrane insertion (Figure 9b–c).
evidence: This is proposed based on the structural analysis.

claim: When interacting with a lipid membrane, aromatic residues at the bottom of the head domain of XaxB likely trigger the conformational change resulting in membrane perforation.
source: When interacting with a lipid membrane, aromatic residues at the bottom of the head domain of XaxB likely trigger the conformational change resulting in membrane perforation (Figure 9d).
evidence: This is proposed based on the structural analysis.

claim: Neither the interaction of the aromatic residues of XaxB nor the hydrophobic domain of XaxA are able to enter membranes on their own.
source: Our reconstitution assays in liposomes showed that neither XaxA nor XaxB strongly interact with liposomes. Thus, neither the interaction of the aromatic residues of XaxB nor the hydrophobic domain of XaxA are able to enter membranes on their own and dimerization and induced conformational changes during oligomerization are crucial for membrane insertion.
evidence: This is inferred from the reconstitution experiments.

claim: Dimerization and induced conformational changes during oligomerization are crucial for membrane insertion.
source: Our reconstitution assays in liposomes showed that neither XaxA nor XaxB strongly interact with liposomes. Thus, neither the interaction of the aromatic residues of XaxB nor the hydrophobic domain of XaxA are able to enter membranes on their own and dimerization and induced conformational changes during oligomerization are crucial for membrane insertion.
evidence: This is inferred from the reconstitution experiments.

claim: Since XaxB is the component that finally forms the pore, XaxA acts like an activator of XaxB and stabilizes it in the pore complex.
source: Since XaxB is the component that finally forms the pore, XaxA that only partially enters the membrane, acts like an activator of XaxB and stabilizes it in the pore complex.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural and functional data.

claim: The crystal structures of YaxA and XaxA are very similar although their sequences are only 54.5% identical.
source: The crystal structures of YaxA and XaxA, as well as YaxB (PaxB) and XaxB are very similar although their sequences are only 54.5 and 36.0% (56.7%) identical, respectively (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a,c,d).
evidence: This is observed by structural comparison.

claim: YaxA does not contain the hook-shaped loop (lp1), which is a prominent feature of XaxA.
source: Importantly, YaxA does not contain the hook-shaped loop (lp1), which is a prominent feature of XaxA (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a,b).
evidence: This is observed by structural comparison.

claim: The YaxAB pore complex comprises 8 to 12 heterodimers in contrast to the 12 to 15 heterodimers in the XaxAB pore.
source: Although the authors used the same detergent for pore assembly and also stabilized the pores in amphipols, the YaxAB pore complex comprises 8 to 12 heterodimers in contrast to the 12 to 15 heterodimers in our XaxAB pore.
evidence: This is observed by comparing the structures.

claim: The difference in pore size between YaxAB and XaxAB suggests a species-dependent size variability.
source: This suggests a species-dependent size variability.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural comparison.

claim: YaxA associates directly with erythrocyte membranes, in contrast to XaxA which does not interact with liposomes in vitro.
source: Interestingly, YaxA associates directly with erythrocyte membranes. This is in direct contrast to our findings showing that XaxA does interact with liposomes in vitro.
evidence: This is based on comparison with the published YaxAB study.

claim: Bräuning et al. hypothesize that YaxA enters the membrane first and then recruits YaxB, whereas the authors propose that XaxA and XaxB already heterodimerize/oligomerize in solution and then associate with the membrane.
source: This results in different models. Whereas Bräuning et al. hypothesize that YaxA enters the membrane first and then recruits YaxB, we propose that XaxA and XaxB already heterodimerize/oligomerize in solution and then associate with the membrane as heterodimers or oligomers.
evidence: This is a comparison of mechanistic models based on different experimental observations.
